https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.title: Cambridge University about-turns on fossil fuel donations – but only if they are big enough
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.subtitle: University scraps temporary ban under new process welcoming sums in ‘exceptional circumstances’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.text:
The University of Cambridge has scrapped a temporary ban on donations from fossil fuel companies and will now accept sums if they are “for a large gift… usually [of] several million pounds”.
The university said it had agreed on a new process for considering funding from fossil fuel companies on Tuesday that would welcome donations under “exceptional circumstances”.
Its committee on benefactions and legal and external affairs (CBELA) may now accept donations if they are “for a large gift, or equivalent value for a research collaboration (usually several million pounds) which could not be obtained elsewhere”.
Funding from such companies must also be shown to advance “the university’s overall academic and institutional aims”.
All other sums must be from companies committed to the UK’s target for reaching net zero by 2050, the university’s website said.
It overrules a temporary ban on fossil fuel donations brought in earlier this year after an independent report warned that due diligence failings had created a “high reputational risk” to the university.
The temporary suspension on funding, which began in March, came after a report by Nigel Topping, the UN climate champion, suggested Cambridge’s association with industry was not worth the reputational risk.
The report found that the fossil fuel sector made up 0.4 per cent of the university’s research and philanthropy funding in the six years up to 2022.
Announcing the move, Cambridge admitted it was “aware” of calls for a “blanket ban” on fossil fuel cash.
However, it said this may “cause tension in relation to academic freedom and freedom of speech” and “give rise to questions” regarding its obligations under charity law.
UK-based oil and gas companies BP and Shell have jointly donated more than £19.7 million to the university since 2019, according to the Financial Times.
Cambridge was also accused of “sidelining ethical considerations” in February when the university took £20 million in funding from Majid Jafar, the owner of the Middle East’s largest oil company.
Mr Jafar is the chief executive and founder of Crescent Petroleum and the managing director of Dana Gas, the largest non-government-owned natural gas company in the Middle East.
The money went towards the development of a Cambridge children’s hospital and university research institute.
The policy will replace existing advice for CBELA, the university’s body for considering donations, which ranked fossil fuel companies red, amber, or green according to their alignment with the Paris Agreement on climate change, The Telegraph understands.
The new process is understood not to have received unanimous support from the university council making the decision. It comprises senior university officials such as Prof Deborah Prentice, the vice-chancellor.
Prof Jason Scott-Warren, one of 25 members of the council, said: “This absurd decision reflects the fundamentally unethical nature of the university, which doesn’t begin to get the climate emergency and which remains densely intertwined with the fossil fuel industry.”
Mr Scott-Warren claimed that despite Mr Topping’s report, Cambridge has decided to ditch the colour-coded donations scale in favour of “these new proposals, which make the size of a donation the decisive factor”.
He said the policy “leaves the door open for multi- million pound donations and collaborations from fossil fuel majors”.
A spokesman for the University of Cambridge said: “The university will not accept research or philanthropic funding from a fossil fuel company whose business model is not aligned with the target of reaching net zero emissions by 2050, unless there are exceptional circumstances.
“No fossil fuel company is currently understood to have a business model that aligns with net zero 2050 targets.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.subtitle: Also from the Front Page newsletter: TV presenter jailed for embezzling £120k of mother’s funds. Sign up below.
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.text:
Good evening. Andy Burnham, the mayor of Greater Manchester, has warned protesters not to exploit the Manchester Airport row for “political purposes”.
Elsewhere in today’s newsletter we cover the jailing of a TV presenter for embezzlement and bring you the latest updates from the US election where Barack Obama is planning to endorse Kamala Harris.
If you want to receive twice-daily briefings like this by email, sign up to the Front Page newsletter here.
Mr Burnham made the comments after a police officer was filmed apparently stamping on a man’s head at the airport on Wednesday.After the clip was widely shared online, hundreds of protesters gathered outside a Rochdale police station on Wednesday night and chanted “Allahu Akbar” – watch footage of this here.
A court heard that 24-year-old Anthony Esan ambushed Lt Col Mark Teeton, a senior Army officer, and repeatedly stabbed him with a set of kitchen knives leaving him with near fatal injuries. The father-of-two was taken to hospital where his condition was said to be serious but stable.
A former STV and BBC presenter has been jailed for more than two years after her sister discovered she had embezzled more than £120,000 from her dementia-stricken mother. Prosecutors have said Hayley Matthews abused her position of trust to “brazenly fund an extravagant lifestyle”.
Social media users have poked fun at a Tom Tugendhat leadership campaign slogan after it accidentally spelt out “TURD”.
Health | The NHS has warned that less than two days’ worth of some types of blood is left following the recent cyber attack. Donors have been urged to come forward and hospitals have been told to restrict the use of the most common types of blood.
Four Russian and Chinese bombers have been intercepted operating together for the first time by US and Canadian fighters near Alaska.
Following a boom in sign-ups to house-sitting services, our writer reveals the highs and lows of living out of other people’s homes.
‘I sent my 64-year-old mum to race Team GB’s fastest man’

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.subtitle: Also from the Front Page newsletter: Winter fuel payments scrapped for millions of pensioners. Sign up below.
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.text:
Good evening. It has been reported that children are among eight people who have been injured in a knife attack in Southport, Merseyside.
Elsewhere in today’s newsletter, Labour has scrapped the universal winter fuel payment for millions of pensioners and Huw Edwards has been charged with making indecent images of children.
Plus: A roundup of all the day’s events at Paris 2024.
If you want to receive twice-daily briefings like this by email, sign up to the Front Page newsletter here.
Armed police and paramedics were called to the Hart Space Studios on Hart Street following reports of “multiple stabbings” at 11.50 am. Eye witnesses described seeing children running into the street covered in blood, with one resident describing the scene like “something in a horror movie” – follow live updates.
Speaking in the Commons, the Chancellor said: “The scale of the situation we are dealing with means incredibly tough choices. I repeat today the commitment that we made in our manifesto to protect the triple lock.“But today I am making the difficult decision that those not in receipt of pension credit or certain other means-tested benefits will no longer receive the winter fuel payment” – follow our live blog here for the latest updates.
The 62-year-old, who left the BBC last year, will appear at Westminster magistrates’ court on Wednesday charged with three offences relating to images shared on WhatsApp. Mr Edwards was arrested last November by detectives from Scotland Yard. He was charged last month.
Conflict | The UK is expected to suspend some arms exports to Israel as early as Tuesday. Two Israeli sources said that Israel is braced for the announcement of a suspension in the coming days, but that the two allies were currently engaged in talks.
By Josh BurrowsDigital Sports Editor
On a glorious Monday, Team GB have their first gold medals of the Paris Olympics.Tom Pidcock, the mountain-biker, rode an astonishing race – recovering 40 seconds after a puncture then pulling off a quite astonishing overtaking move on his French rival in the closing kilometre. He was booed afterwards by French fans.Earlier today, after winning the team eventing title, Laura Collett said she hoped the gold medal would bring an end to the equestrian scandal that dominated the build-up to these games. “Our horses don’t perform like that if they are not happy,” she said. Collett also won individual bronze.There was also an emotional silver medal for Tom Daley, in front of his young family in the synchronised diving.More GB medals could yet follow this afternoon in the men’s team gymnastics and the 200m freestyle swimming.
Swifties packed the Olympic Hill, or Olympiaberg, to get a view of the sold-out concert.
British writer and film producer Kate Wilson discovered she had advanced ovarian cancer when she decided to donate a kidney.
